claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has notable strength and fatigue performance.
High-temperature degradation of the target alloy is governed by segregation of Al, Cr, and Ti to grain boundaries and interfacial regions.
In oxidizing atmospheres, segregation of Al, Cr, and Ti drives formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale preserves the mechanical integrity of the underlying FCC alloy.
In reducing atmospheres, protective oxide formation is absent or existing oxides are reduced.
Failure to sustain a protective scale in reducing atmospheres causes internal oxidation and degradation.
Slight changes in Al, Cr, or Ti content will alter grain-boundary segregation behavior.
Grain boundaries and second-phase interfaces are the relevant locations at which reactive-element segregation controls oxide-scale formation and adherence.
Alumina- and chromia-type oxides form the proposed continuous, adherent protective layer.
Oxide reduction or inadequate scale formation under reducing conditions compromises intergranular cohesion.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a well-adherent, continuous scale with minimal internal damage in the baseline alloy.
After oxidizing exposure, the baseline alloy will retain its mechanical properties.
Reducing exposure will cause grain-boundary or internal oxidation and measurable losses in strength and fatigue behavior.
Variants with reduced availability or segregation of Al, Cr, or Ti will form poorer oxide scales in oxidizing atmospheres.
Variants with reduced availability or segregation of Al, Cr, or Ti will undergo greater degradation in reducing atmospheres.
The proposed segregation-controlled mechanism applies over 700–900 °C when exposure is long enough for oxide-scale evolution.
The quantitative kinetics, relative contributions of Al, Cr, and Ti, and protective-to-deleterious oxygen-partial-pressure threshold are not established.
